prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I put circuit QED first in my opening ballot, and I still think it is the cleanest new regime of light-matter interaction of the last twenty years. After hearing colleagues, though, I am moving my preferred configuration to the optical lattice clock. Five of six members who ranked it placed it in their top three, and the scientific case is strong on the criteria I care about. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes Doppler and recoil shifts for thousands of atoms at once. Ye's group turned it into the most accurate and stable clocks yet built. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) now operate clocks at the 10^-18 level and compare them, so the result is robust and reproducible. This is a controlled quantum system that opened a new measurement regime, with concrete consequences: relativistic redshift over millimetres, constraints on varying constants, dark-matter searches and the pending redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist. The discovery, not the application, is what we reward, and here the discovery is a concrete, measured one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee has rewarded the neighbouring ground twice already: Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, control of single quantum systems and ion clocks). A critic can say the lattice clock is a refinement of a rewarded program rather than a new discovery. Credit is also not perfectly clean, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others did early lattice-clock work outside the credited names, and the SI second has not yet been redefined. I regard these as real but manageable. The magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea, and the 10^-18 accuracy is something the earlier prizes did not deliver.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because they are the clearest case of a new measurement technique with quantitative, cross-checked evidence, but flags the possible overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He ranks circuit QED sixth because a second superconducting-circuit award right after 2025 looks unlikely.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and partly with the second. The evidence for lattice clocks is exactly of the cross-laboratory kind I trust, and I think the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is smaller than it looks: neither prize covers the magic-wavelength scheme or the 10^-18 regime. On circuit QED, I accept the timing argument. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, and cQED is a different discovery, namely strong single-photon coupling and dispersive readout. But the Academy would reasonably not want two superconducting-circuit prizes within a year or two, and I would not push B005 against that concern.

responses.point: Pearce ranks circuit QED last of his eight, because the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits overlaps in subject, and he defers to colleagues on this field.
responses.response: Since I work in this field, let me say what I think is fair. The two discoveries are different: tunnelling and level quantisation in a single junction (2025), versus coupling an artificial atom to a single photon in a resonator and reading it out dispersively. But I take the point that to the Academy and the public both read as superconducting circuits. I also note that Pearce ranks lattice clocks fourth and describes the attribution as clean, so there is a path to agreement between us on B012, which is where I now stand. I would keep circuit QED as an alternative for a later year, not this one.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a theory-then-experiment story with clear clues from nature, strongly confirmed across many groups, and ranks lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation is a compelling story, and it is a field that has clearly opened a new regime. My reservation is the one I held when I ranked it sixth: the interpretation is not yet stable. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, sample-to-sample and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility, and Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, is outside the credited names. This is outside my core expertise, so I defer to you and Eriksson on the condensed-matter side. But for me the lattice clock has a more settled physical picture, and I would accept B042 as a fully respectable outcome if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and topological insulators third, valuing a predicted state realised in a clean tunable platform and a mature, verified discovery.
responses.response: On topological insulators, I ranked B030 fourth and share your view that it is mature and well verified. My concern, which you also state, is the attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum wells that Molenkamp's group then measured, and the 3D case (Fu-Kane, Moore-Balents, Hasan) is also outside the supplied three names. The 2016 prize on topological phases adds some overlap. I do not think this is disqualifying, but it makes B030 a harder configuration to defend than lattice clocks to me. If you think the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio can be defended as the central chain of prediction and observation, I would like to hear how you handle Zhang.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first as precision atomic physics where credit separation from the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes is manageable, and treats Rydberg arrays as impressive but not yet a completed discovery.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and you know the atomic-physics priorities better than I do. Your remark that credit separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is manageable is the key one for my move to B012. On Rydberg arrays I share your judgement of maturity: I ranked B019 seventh because it still looks like a platform in rapid development, and the credit is spread across Bernien, Endres, Greiner, Weiss and others, besides Zoller and Jaksch. I would not raise it this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which I cannot settle alone.
Whether Katori's and Ye's contributions are the right pair, given early lattice-clock work by Lemonde, Takamoto and others; I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on atomic-physics priority.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited before awarding.
Whether a circuit QED prize would be viewed as acceptable in a year or two after 2025, which affects how I rank B005 in later rounds.
Whether trapped-ion quantum computation (B020) can be credited without leaving out Wineland and Monroe, given the 2012 prize.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of WACQT (Chalmers), a national programme in superconducting quantum computing, and I work professionally in circuit QED. This is a field-proximity and possible institutional interest in B005 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf), and to a lesser extent B020 and B019 as quantum-computing platforms, and I opened with B005 first for that reason I flag it for possible recusal or discounting on B005. My profile shows no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, so no specific conflict is apparent for my preferred B012.
